questions.stem: Which element is essential to a problem definition but absent from a project brief that merely describes the desired system?
options: A list of the technologies to be used
The names of the development team
A measurable statement of the current state and the target state
The chosen development approach
questions.explanation: "6 minutes per booking and a 12% double-booking rate, reduced to under 1 minute and zero" is what makes success testable later. Technology choices belong to a later phase.

questions.stem: Defining what is explicitly out of scope primarily protects against:
options: Budget miscalculation
Technical infeasibility
Poor requirements gathering
Scope creep, by making later additions visibly a change rather than an assumption
questions.explanation: Exclusions are what make a change-request conversation possible — without them every addition can be argued to have been implied.

questions.stem: A success criterion of "the system will be easy to use" fails because it:
options: Is not relevant to the client
Cannot be objectively tested as met or unmet
Describes a functional rather than performance requirement
Belongs in the testing phase
questions.explanation: "Task completion at least 90% and time to complete a booking under 60 seconds" is the same intention made measurable.

questions.stem: A project's constraints are best documented at which stage?
options: Testing and evaluating
Researching and planning
Producing and implementing
Identifying and defining
questions.explanation: Budget, time, technology and legal constraints bound every subsequent decision — discovering them during the build is a leading cause of rework.

questions.stem: Which is a stakeholder but not a user of a school booking system?
options: A student making a booking
A teacher checking the daily schedule
The privacy regulator whose requirements the system must satisfy
An administrator maintaining the room list
questions.explanation: Stakeholders include anyone affected by or with an interest in the system, which is broader than the set of people who operate it.

questions.stem: Missing a stakeholder during requirements gathering most typically produces:
options: A system that meets the specification but not the actual need
A system that fails verification
A system that cannot be tested
A system with poor performance
questions.explanation: That is a validation failure — the build is correct against a specification that was itself wrong.

questions.stem: The Gantt chart's principal contribution beyond a task list is that it shows:
options: Who is responsible for each task
Duration, dependencies, overlap, milestones and the critical path
The budget allocated to each task
The acceptance criteria for each deliverable
questions.explanation: Owners (A) can appear on a task list; the temporal and dependency structure is what only a Gantt chart makes visible.

questions.stem: A task with three weeks of float slips by four weeks. The consequence is:
options: No effect on the project end date
The critical path is recalculated to exclude the task
The whole project is delayed by four weeks
The task becomes critical and the project end date slips by one week
questions.explanation: Float absorbs delay only up to its length — this is exactly the arithmetic a stimulus question tests.

questions.stem: Which is not shown on a standard Gantt chart?
options: Milestones
The logical flow of data between processes
Task dependencies
Percentage complete
questions.explanation: Data flow is a DFD's job. Confusing the purpose of planning tools with modelling tools is a common and costly error.

questions.stem: A PERT/network diagram is preferred over a Gantt chart when the priority is:
options: Reporting progress visually to a client
Allocating budget across work packages
Showing calendar dates for each task
Computing the critical path and float from the dependency network
questions.explanation: The two are complements: PERT emphasises the dependency structure, Gantt emphasises calendar time and progress reporting.

questions.stem: Resource levelling addresses:
options: Insufficient project budget
Unclear task dependencies
Over-allocation of a person or resource across concurrent tasks
Excessive float in the schedule
questions.explanation: A schedule assuming one developer works 160% of a week is a forecast of a missed deadline rather than a plan.

questions.stem: Which process diary entry demonstrates the reflective element assessors look for?
options: "Tuesday: chose a junction table over a repeating group for enrolments, because the repeating group would have broken reporting by subject; accepted the extra join cost."
"Tuesday: worked on the database."
"Tuesday: completed 8 hours of development."
"Tuesday: met with the client."
questions.explanation: Dated activity plus the decision and its justification. The others record that time passed, not that development was managed.

questions.stem: A budget that omits ongoing operating costs is defective because:
options: Lifetime cost is dominated by operation and maintenance, so the comparison between options becomes misleading
It cannot be presented to a client
Contingency cannot be calculated without it
It breaches accounting standards
questions.explanation: A cheaper build with a higher licence and support cost frequently loses over three years — which the build-only figure conceals.

questions.stem: Typical project contingency is around:
questions.explanation: 10–15% — Too little and any surprise becomes a crisis; too much and the estimate stops being a discipline.

questions.stem: The difference between iteration and increment is that iteration:
options: Adds new pieces while increment refines existing ones
Refers to sprints while increment refers to releases
Applies only to Agile and increment only to Waterfall
Refines the same thing while increment adds new pieces
questions.explanation: (A) is the pair inverted. Agile typically does both within each cycle.

questions.stem: "Follow-the-sun" development delivers value by:
options: Reducing the total number of developer hours required
Removing the need for documentation
Eliminating communication overhead
Using time-zone differences so work continues around the clock
questions.explanation: It increases communication and handover overhead, which is the balancing cost that (C) inverts.

questions.stem: The most significant data governance concern with offshore development is:
options: Personal data crossing borders into a different legal jurisdiction, engaging cross-border disclosure obligations
Higher labour costs in the destination country
A smaller available talent pool
Slower internet connectivity
questions.explanation: Under APP 8 the Australian entity generally remains accountable for what an overseas recipient does with the data.

questions.stem: The security concern most specific to remote working is:
options: Reduced team cohesion
Difficulty scheduling meetings
Home networks and personal devices sitting outside enterprise security controls
Higher software licensing costs
questions.explanation: (A) is a genuine cost of remote work but is a collaboration issue, not a security one — the question tests the category.

questions.stem: A frequently cited non-security cost of remote work is:
options: Reduced access to the talent pool
Higher office rental costs
Increased commuting emissions
Weaker spontaneous collaboration and reduced mentoring of junior staff
questions.explanation: (B), (C) and (A) are all inverted — remote work reduces office cost and commuting and widens the talent pool.

questions.stem: From the enterprise's perspective, the principal risk of freelance and gig arrangements is:
options: Variable quality, availability risk, and knowledge leaving at project end
Higher long-term overhead
Inability to access specialist skills
Slower scaling of team size
questions.explanation: (B), (C) and (D) invert the model's advantages, which is what makes them plausible if the trade-off is half-remembered.

questions.stem: Cloud service models enable start-ups principally by:
options: Guaranteeing lower total cost over five years
Removing the need for software developers
Converting infrastructure capital expenditure into operating expenditure
Providing free marketing distribution
questions.explanation: Total cost at scale is often higher in the cloud — the advantage is that no capital is required to start, which is a different claim.

questions.stem: The net effect of these changes on competition is best described as:
options: Lower barriers to entry, increasing competition and innovation but also failure rates and platform dependence
Higher barriers to entry, favouring incumbents
No material change in market structure
Benefits confined to large enterprises
questions.explanation: A balanced statement naming both sides is what an analyse or discuss verb requires.

questions.stem: The primary project benefit of online collaboration tools is:
options: Eliminating the need for meetings
Automatic generation of documentation
A single source of truth with version history and an audit trail of decisions
Guaranteed data security
questions.explanation: The named risks are tool sprawl, notification overload, access control and dependence on connectivity.

questions.stem: In a system flowchart, a trapezium represents:
options: A manual operation
A decision
A stored data file
A document
questions.explanation: Manual operation — A wavy-bottom rectangle is a document and a cylinder is stored data — system flowcharts include the human steps, which is what distinguishes them from program flowcharts.

questions.stem: A system flowchart differs from a DFD because it shows:
options: Only automated processes
Only the data stores used
Sequence and control flow, including manual steps, hardware and documents
The class hierarchy of the solution
questions.explanation: DFDs show where data goes, not when. Sequence is the flowchart's contribution.

questions.stem: In a DFD, a process must be named using:
options: A noun describing the data it holds
The database table it reads from
The name of the department responsible
A verb and object, such as "Process Order"
questions.explanation: Processes are numbered and verb-phrased; nouns belong on data stores and external entities.

questions.stem: Balancing between DFD levels requires that:
options: Each level contain the same number of processes
Each process be decomposed to the same depth
The external entities and net flows crossing the system boundary be identical
Data stores appear at every level
questions.explanation: Level 1 adds internal detail only — data stores are absent at Level 0 by convention, which is why (D) is wrong.

questions.stem: A Level 1 DFD introduces a new external entity not present at Level 0. This is:
options: Acceptable if the entity is labelled
A black hole
Required when data stores are added
A balancing error
questions.explanation: The system boundary is fixed at Level 0 — a new external input means the scope changed, which must be resolved rather than drawn.

questions.stem: A "miracle" or grey hole in a DFD is:
options: A data store connected to an external entity
A process with inputs but no outputs
A process producing output with no matching input
An unlabelled data flow
questions.explanation: (B) is a black hole — the mirror-image error, and the pair are routinely confused.

questions.stem: Data flows in a DFD should be labelled with:
options: The action performed on the data
The process number at each end
The frequency of transmission
The name of the data moving
questions.explanation: "Booking request", not "sends booking" — the label names the payload, not the verb.

questions.stem: Which activity best demonstrates systems thinking in a project?
options: Designing the database schema efficiently
Recognising that the new booking system changes rostering, inventory and customer expectations
Interviewing users to understand their frustrations
Writing precise algorithm steps for the pricing logic
questions.explanation: (A) and (D) are computational thinking and (C) is design thinking — the three are used together and are commonly conflated.

questions.stem: Design thinking's Define stage produces:
options: A working prototype
A test plan
A list of technical requirements
A point-of-view statement aligning the user need with the business objective
questions.explanation: It sits between Empathise and Ideate, and it is what prevents ideation from drifting away from the observed need.

questions.stem: Prototyping "low fidelity first" is recommended because:
options: Low-fidelity prototypes are quicker to produce
Rough artefacts invite critique of structure and flow, while polished ones attract comment on colour and imply progress
High-fidelity prototypes cannot be tested with users
Low fidelity is required before high fidelity in every methodology
questions.explanation: Speed (A) is real but secondary — the behavioural effect on the feedback you receive is the substantive reason.

questions.stem: MoSCoW prioritisation is most valuable because it:
options: Estimates the duration of each requirement
Assigns each requirement to a developer
Separates needs from wants, giving the client a structured way to trade scope against time and budget
Determines the development approach
questions.explanation: It converts an unstructured argument about features into a negotiation with an agreed vocabulary.

questions.stem: In a RACI matrix, exactly one person should be:
options: Responsible
Informed
Consulted
Accountable
questions.explanation: Accountable — Multiple people may be responsible for doing the work, but shared accountability is effectively no accountability.

questions.stem: Quality assurance requires all of the following except:
options: Measurable quality criteria defined early
Continual checking against requirements throughout development
Addressing compliance and legislative requirements
A single comprehensive inspection at project completion
questions.explanation: QA is continual, which is precisely what distinguishes it from a final quality control inspection.

questions.stem: "Designing for ease of maintenance" is justified primarily because:
options: Maintenance is typically the largest lifetime cost and is usually performed by someone other than the author
Maintenance is the smallest cost in the lifecycle
It reduces the initial build time
It is required for client sign-off
questions.explanation: Modular structure, meaningful naming, documentation and separated configuration all reduce total cost of ownership.

questions.stem: Which requirements tool is best for uncovering needs users cannot articulate?
options: A prototype users can react to
A survey with closed questions
An analytical report on existing system usage
A budget review
questions.explanation: Its named risks are that users mistake it for a finished product and fixate on visuals — which is why low fidelity is preferred early.

questions.stem: Analytical reports from existing system data are limited because they:
options: Impose a burden on participants
Require a large sample to be valid
Cannot be quantified
Reveal what happened but not why, and may be defined for another purpose
questions.explanation: Their strength is objectivity and zero participant burden — (A) inverts that, which is what makes it a plausible distractor.

questions.stem: Waterfall is most defensible when:
options: Requirements will evolve as the client sees the product
The team is exploring an unfamiliar problem domain
The client wants working software every fortnight
Requirements are stable and the project is regulated, safety-critical or fixed-price
questions.explanation: Waterfall buys certainty of cost and scope at the price of flexibility; Agile buys flexibility at the price of certainty.

questions.stem: Agile's most commonly cited weakness for a fixed-price contract is:
options: Poor code quality
Excessive documentation
Insufficient user involvement
Difficulty fixing scope, cost and delivery date up front
questions.explanation: Thin documentation is a real risk too, but the contractual tension is what makes Agile awkward for fixed-price work specifically.

questions.stem: Evolutionary prototyping's characteristic risk is:
options: The prototype is discarded, wasting effort
Users cannot provide feedback on a working model
A proof of concept becomes production without ever being engineered for it
It cannot be used for UI-heavy systems
questions.explanation: (A) describes the throwaway variant's cost — the two approaches carry opposite risks, which is the distinction being tested.

questions.stem: End-user development's most persistent structural risk is:
options: Excessive documentation slowing delivery
Weak security, validation and version control, with key-person dependency when the builder leaves
High licensing costs
Slow initial delivery
questions.explanation: The critical spreadsheet nobody in IT knows exists is the classic manifestation — "shadow IT".

questions.stem: Outsourcing is least defensible when the system is:
options: A non-core internal utility
Outside the internal team's skill set
Needed within a tight deadline
Close to the enterprise's competitive advantage
questions.explanation: Loss of internal knowledge and vendor lock-in matter most where the system is strategically central.

questions.stem: A storyboard's distinctive contribution is that it:
options: Documents the database structure
Shows the user journey and screen flow frame by frame, exposing missing steps
Sequences tasks and their dependencies
Defines the test data categories
questions.explanation: It surfaces "what happens if they have no account?" while change still costs nothing.

questions.stem: Risk is assessed on a matrix as:
options: Cost multiplied by duration
Probability divided by budget
Likelihood multiplied by consequence
Impact multiplied by float
questions.explanation: Treat by zone: extreme → avoid, high → reduce, medium → transfer, low → accept and monitor.

questions.stem: Transferring a risk through insurance transfers:
options: The full consequence including reputational damage
Responsibility for the control
The likelihood of the event occurring
Financial consequence only, not reputational harm or legal obligations
questions.explanation: Naming what transfer does not cover is what turns a definition into an evaluation.

questions.stem: For a risk rated extreme, the appropriate treatment is:
options: Accept and monitor with contingency budget
Avoid — do not proceed, or change the approach
Transfer through insurance
Reduce through additional controls
questions.explanation: Extreme risks are not manageable by controls alone; the activity itself must change.

questions.stem: Data migration verification should include:
options: Deleting the source system immediately after cutover
Converting all fields to text to avoid type errors
Comparing record counts and checksums, and spot-checking business-critical fields
Skipping validation to meet the cutover window
questions.explanation: Staged migration with a documented rollback path is the standard risk treatment for this activity.

questions.stem: Training is best scheduled:
options: Immediately before go-live, with ongoing support and updated documentation afterwards
Six months before go-live, to allow time for practice
Three months after go-live, once users have identified their needs
Only for super-users, who then train others informally
questions.explanation: Training too early decays before it is used; too late and the business disrupts. Floor-walking support in week one converts training into competence.

questions.stem: Direct cutover is defensible when:
options: The data is irreplaceable and the system is safety-critical
The new system differs radically from the old
The organisation operates across many geographically separate sites
The consequence of failure is low, the system is simple, and parallel running would cost more than the risk it removes
questions.explanation: The decision turns on consequence of failure, not on cost — which is why (A) and (B) point toward parallel or phased.

questions.stem: Parallel conversion's principal cost is:
options: A prolonged period of temporary interfaces between old and new
Doubled workload and data entry, with associated staff fatigue
Delayed realisation of benefits at sites not yet converted
No fallback if the new system fails
questions.explanation: Running both systems means every transaction is entered twice, with the associated fatigue and error risk. The other options belong to phased, pilot and direct respectively.

questions.stem: Phased conversion introduces which characteristic complication?
options: A single high-risk cutover moment
Temporary interfaces between old and new modules during a long transition
An unrepresentative trial population
Doubled data entry across the whole organisation
questions.explanation: Risk is contained per module and training is spread out, at the cost of duration and interim complexity.

questions.stem: Pilot conversion's characteristic weakness is:
options: There is no fallback if the pilot fails
The pilot site may not represent the wider organisation
Staff must enter data twice
The transition period is indefinite
questions.explanation: Choosing a pilot site that is unusually capable or unusually simple produces a rollout confidently based on a false result.

questions.stem: Verification asks whether the system:
options: Matches the specification
Meets the user's actual need
Performs adequately under load
Conforms to accessibility standards
questions.explanation: A system can pass verification and fail validation — it does exactly what the specification said, and the specification was wrong.

questions.stem: User acceptance testing primarily achieves:
options: Verification against the design documents
Validation against the users' actual need and the original success criteria
Performance measurement under peak load
Security assurance against injection attacks
questions.explanation: It is the gateway to sign-off, which is why it must be conducted by users rather than developers.

questions.stem: In the V-model, system testing corresponds to which design stage?
options: Problem definition
High-level design
System requirements
Detailed design
questions.explanation: UAT ↔ problem definition, system testing ↔ requirements, integration ↔ high-level design, unit ↔ detailed design.

questions.stem: For a field accepting values 1 to 100, which set is boundary data?
options: "abc", −5, blank
questions.explanation: On and immediately either side of each limit. (A) is normal, (B) abnormal and (D) extreme — all four categories appear as options.

questions.stem: Abnormal test data confirms that the system:
options: Operates correctly under typical conditions
Performs within response-time targets
Rejects invalid input gracefully with a helpful message rather than crashing
Handles the largest expected volume
questions.explanation: Extreme data — values far beyond the expected range — is what confirms the system does not crash, which is the adjacent category.

questions.stem: Good test data must above all be:
options: As voluminous as possible
Drawn from live production records
Traceable to a requirement, with a documented expected result
Randomly generated to avoid developer bias
questions.explanation: Without a documented expected result you are running the software, not testing it — there is nothing to compare against.

questions.stem: Using live production data for testing carries which specific risk?
options: It cannot expose real-world anomalies
It is too clean to be useful
Privacy exposure and possible corruption of production records
It cannot be automated
questions.explanation: Use a de-identified copy in a sandbox — never production. Simulated data is safe and lets you construct edge cases deliberately.

questions.stem: Regression testing exists to confirm that:
options: The system performs under peak load
A change has not broken previously working functionality
Every logical path executes at least once
Users can complete their tasks efficiently
questions.explanation: It is what makes an automated suite pay for itself — manual regression becomes impossible as a system grows.

questions.stem: Which approach properly trials the operation and maintenance documentation?
options: Someone other than the author to follow it and complete real tasks
The author to re-read it after a break
A spelling and grammar review
Publication in an accessible format
questions.explanation: The author cannot detect their own assumed knowledge — which is the whole point of the exercise.

questions.stem: Responding to a change in privacy legislation by updating the system is which maintenance type?
options: Corrective
Preventive
Perfective
Adaptive
questions.explanation: Adaptive — responding to a changed environment. Corrective fixes defects, perfective improves or enhances, preventive refactors before problems occur.

questions.stem: Refactoring and updating dependencies before any fault occurs is:
options: Corrective
Adaptive
Perfective
Preventive
questions.explanation: Preventive — It is the maintenance category most often cut from budgets and most reliably regretted.

questions.stem: Reviewing implementation impact should cover:
options: Technical, organisational, user, financial, legal/ethical and environmental dimensions
Technical performance only
Financial return only
User satisfaction only
questions.explanation: Naming all six domains structures an extended response and demonstrates systems thinking.

questions.stem: A traceability matrix links:
options: Each requirement to its test and result
Risks to their owners
Tables to their foreign keys
Tasks to their dependencies
questions.explanation: It is the direct evidence for the functionality criterion — every requirement demonstrably tested and passed.

questions.stem: The strongest evaluation criterion for an online booking system is:
options: "Handling time fell from 6 minutes to 48 seconds against a 60-second target; double-booking rate 0% against a 0% target"
"Users found the interface attractive"
"The system was delivered on schedule"
"The client expressed satisfaction"
questions.explanation: Evaluation must return to the measurable success criteria set in the problem definition — closing that loop is what earns marks.

questions.stem: A client requests four extra features with no change to deadline or budget. The best response is:
options: Assess and document the time and cost impact, present options, and obtain written agreement
Absorb the work to preserve the relationship
Decline without explanation
Deliver the features by reducing the testing phase
questions.explanation: Making the trade-off visible keeps the decision with the client. (D) is how projects fail quietly.

questions.stem: A hospital medication system is replacing an existing one. The defensible conversion method is:
options: Parallel or carefully staged phased, because the consequence of failure is patient harm
Direct, to minimise cost and duration
End-user development by the nursing staff
Pilot across every ward simultaneously
questions.explanation: The cost of running both systems is trivial relative to the consequence of a medication error — criticality dominates.

questions.stem: A team adopts Agile but the client is unavailable for the term. The predictable outcome is:
options: Faster delivery, since fewer meetings are required
Reduced technical debt
Improved documentation quality
The core benefit of continuous validated feedback is lost, and the team builds on assumptions in short bursts
questions.explanation: Approach selection must account for the client's capacity, not only the team's preference.

questions.stem: A completed system passes all tests but staff say it does not match how they actually work. The failure occurred at:
options: Testing and evaluating
Researching and planning
Producing and implementing
Identifying and defining, where requirements were gathered from the wrong stakeholders
questions.explanation: Requirements gathered from managers rather than the people doing the work is the classic cause — and it surfaces only at validation.

questions.stem: A Gantt chart shows every task complete but user acceptance testing has not begun. The likely explanation is:
options: The project is genuinely finished
The critical path was miscalculated
Testing was never scheduled as work with duration and owners, or progress is being reported inaccurately
There was too much float in the schedule
questions.explanation: Testing and evaluating is a project stage, not an activity that happens after the work.

questions.stem: The strongest evidence of managed development for an assessor is:
options: A large and functional finished product
Planned versus actual on time and cost, a dated decision log with justifications, and evidence of feedback changing decisions
Well-commented source code
A comprehensive final report
questions.explanation: Planned versus actual is the core evidence that development was managed rather than merely occurring.

questions.stem: A prototype receives enthusiastic feedback and the client assumes the project is nearly complete. The best mitigation is:
options: Set expectations explicitly about what is simulated versus built, and keep early prototypes deliberately low fidelity
Stop showing prototypes to the client
Increase the polish so the client sees genuine quality
Provide a written progress percentage instead
questions.explanation: (C) worsens the problem — the more finished it looks, the stronger the false impression of progress.

questions.stem: A team proposes skipping documentation to meet a deadline. The strongest counter-argument is:
options: Maintenance dominates lifetime cost, and undocumented systems create key-person dependency and expensive rework
Documentation is a legal requirement in all projects
Documentation improves runtime performance
Clients always read technical documentation
questions.explanation: The saving is realised once; the cost recurs every month afterwards.

questions.stem: "The lead developer may resign" is which risk category, and how is it best treated?
options: Technical; add redundant hardware
External; change supplier
Financial; increase the contingency budget
Project; treat by cross-training, documentation and knowledge sharing
questions.explanation: Key-person dependency is reduced by changing how the team works, not by purchasing insurance against it.

questions.stem: A new system substantially changes staff workflows. The greatest operational risk is:
options: Insufficient server capacity
Inappropriate chart selection in reports
Poor database normalisation
User resistance and inadequate training causing disruption at cutover
questions.explanation: Treated through change management, early involvement of affected staff, super-users, timely training and a safer conversion method.

questions.stem: The strongest reason to schedule a post-implementation review before go-live is:
options: It satisfies the client's reporting requirements
It reduces the cost of the review
A review with no committed date is a review that never happens
It allows the team to be disbanded earlier
questions.explanation: Committing the date and the criteria in the implementation plan is what converts intention into practice.

questions.stem: A client requests a system in 6 weeks that realistically requires 16. The professional response is:
options: Agree and manage expectations later
Present the evidence-based estimate, then offer a reduced-scope deliverable achievable in 6 weeks with a phased roadmap
Decline the project
Compress testing and documentation to fit
questions.explanation: Negotiating scope rather than compressing quality is the professional move, and it maps directly onto MoSCoW.

questions.stem: For an outsourced build, the most commonly omitted and most consequential contract term is:
options: The vendor's registered address
Exit and transition arrangements
The number of developers assigned
The preferred programming language
questions.explanation: Vendor lock-in is realised at the moment you try to leave — which is precisely when it is too late to negotiate.

questions.stem: Which best demonstrates ongoing evaluation rather than end-of-project evaluation?
options: A final report submitted after go-live
The client's satisfaction survey
A single UAT session before sign-off
Iteration-by-iteration assessment against the criteria, with a record of what changed as a result
questions.explanation: Evaluation that never changes a decision is documentation. The record of consequent change is what makes it evaluation.

questions.stem: Users make frequent errors despite the system meeting every requirement. The correct interpretation is:
options: Users need more training and the design is sound
Persistent user error is usually a design signal — usability test, modify under change control, then regression test
The requirements were too detailed
The error rate should be accepted as normal
questions.explanation: "Error prevention over error messages" — modifying designs to improve functionality is an explicit part of the final stage.

questions.stem: Which pairing of stage and artefact is correct?
options: Researching and planning — DFDs, storyboards and the development approach decision
Identifying and defining — Gantt chart and DFDs
Producing and implementing — feasibility study and scope statement
Testing and evaluating — SMART requirements
questions.explanation: Feasibility, scope and SMART requirements belong to identifying and defining; the Gantt chart and modelling tools to researching and planning.

questions.stem: A structure chart's filled circle denotes:
options: A data item passed downward
A result returned upward
A control flag
A module boundary
questions.explanation: Control flag — Data down and results up are both labelled arrows — the filled circle specifically signals control rather than data.

questions.stem: On a class diagram, inheritance is shown by:
options: A filled diamond from parent to subclass
A dashed line with an open arrowhead
A hollow triangle arrow from subclass to parent
A solid line with no arrowhead
questions.explanation: The direction matters — subclass to parent — and markers reward correct standard notation explicitly.

questions.stem: Which risk treatment is appropriate for a low-rated risk?
options: Avoid by changing the approach
Transfer through insurance
Accept, log it, and hold contingency
Reduce through additional controls
questions.explanation: Treating every risk as if it were extreme consumes the budget and attention that genuinely extreme risks require.

questions.stem: Which statement about the four project phases is most accurate?
options: They are strictly sequential and never revisited
They are iterative, with findings from testing feeding back into defining, planning and producing
Only the first two require documentation
Testing occurs before planning in an Agile project
questions.explanation: The feedback arrows are the point of the diagram — and the process diary runs across all four.

questions.stem: An implementation plan omits go/no-go criteria. The consequence at cutover is:
options: The decision to proceed becomes a judgement call under pressure, with no agreed threshold or rollback trigger
Training will be delayed
The budget cannot be finalised
The Gantt chart cannot be completed
questions.explanation: Criteria agreed in advance, when nobody is under pressure, are what make a no-go decision possible at all.

questions.stem: A project's stakeholders disagree about a requirement. The most appropriate response is:
options: Implement both interpretations
Facilitate a negotiation, document the agreed outcome, and record it as a decision with its rationale
Defer to the most senior stakeholder without discussion
Postpone the requirement to a later release without notification
questions.explanation: Negotiating and documenting is explicitly a named communication issue in this module.

questions.stem: Which is the strongest justification structure for a development approach?
options: Name the most widely used approach in the industry
State criteria — requirement stability, size, client availability, team skills, regulatory need — evaluate, and say why the alternatives are worse
Describe each approach in turn
Choose whichever approach the client requests
questions.explanation: "Justify" specifically requires the rejection of alternatives; description caps at the lower bands.

questions.stem: A risk is identified late in the project that was foreseeable at planning. The process failure is:
options: Insufficient contingency budget
The risk should have been transferred
The risk matrix used the wrong scale
Risk identification was treated as a one-off exercise rather than a monitored, recurring activity
questions.explanation: The cycle is identify → assess → treat → monitor, with new risks emerging throughout and feeding back to identification.

questions.stem: An evaluation reports only that "the client was satisfied". The weakness is:
options: Client satisfaction is irrelevant to project success
Satisfaction cannot be measured
It is one criterion among several, with no measurement against pre-defined criteria and no evidence
Only quantitative criteria are acceptable
questions.explanation: Add functional coverage, performance measurement, test results, accessibility conformance and usage data.

questions.stem: The three levels of testing build on each other because:
options: Integration assumes the units already pass, and system testing assumes the integrations do
Each level replaces the previous one
They can be conducted in any order
Only system testing is required for sign-off
questions.explanation: Which is why stubs and drivers exist — so unit and integration testing can begin before every component is finished.

questions.stem: Shipping a defect fix without re-running earlier tests risks:
options: A compilation failure
An outdated data dictionary
A regression that nothing is watching for
An inaccurate Gantt chart
questions.explanation: The fix is verified; the surrounding behaviour is not — which is precisely the scenario regression testing exists to cover.

questions.stem: A team must decide between building in-house and buying a SaaS product. The decisive criterion is usually:
options: Which option is cheaper in year one
Which option the vendor recommends
Which option uses more modern technology
Whether the process is core to competitive advantage and whether internal capability exists to maintain it
questions.explanation: Year-one cost (A) systematically favours SaaS and ignores lock-in and fit — which is why it is a poor sole criterion.

questions.stem: A stimulus describes a low-stakes internal tool with a tight budget. The best-matched implementation method is:
options: Parallel across all departments
Direct cutover
Pilot across six sites over six months
Phased over 18 months
questions.explanation: Right-sizing the method to the risk is the judgement being tested — the same reasoning that rules direct cutover out for payroll.

questions.stem: In a scenario question, the single highest-value action is to:
options: Reference the specific system, users, data or constraints from the stimulus in every point made
Define every technical term used
List all four implementation methods
Recommend the most modern technology available
questions.explanation: Generic, technically correct answers that ignore the stimulus are the most-cited marker complaint across every module.

questions.stem: The most defensible way to demonstrate a solution met its purpose is:
options: A screenshot of the finished interface
The client's written thanks
A list of technologies and libraries used
Reporting each original measurable criterion against the achieved result
questions.explanation: Closing the loop back to the criteria set in the problem definition is what turns a description into an evaluation.

questions.stem: A change is made without updating the documentation. The most serious consequence appears:
options: Immediately, when the change is deployed
During maintenance, when the next person relies on documentation that no longer matches the system
During testing, when the change fails
At sign-off, when the client reviews the deliverables
questions.explanation: Documentation that is subtly wrong is more dangerous than documentation that is obviously absent, because it is trusted.

questions.stem: Which best demonstrates the justify verb applied to a conversion method?
options: "Parallel conversion was used."
"Parallel conversion runs both systems simultaneously."
"Parallel conversion is the safest method available."

"Parallel was chosen because the payroll data is irreplaceable and a failed cutover would prevent staff being paid; direct was rejected for having no fallback, and phased because payroll cannot be run half in each system."
questions.explanation: Decision, reasons, evidence, and explicit rejection of the alternatives — that last element is what "justify" specifically demands.

questions.stem: A project team records every decision but never revisits any of them. The weakness is:
options: A decision log supports evaluation only if superseded decisions are reviewed and updated as circumstances change
The record is too detailed to be useful
Decisions should not be recorded before implementation
The log duplicates the Gantt chart
questions.explanation: Ongoing evaluation requires the record to be live rather than archival.

questions.stem: Which is the strongest indicator that a requirement is not testable?
options: No measurable threshold or observable outcome is specified
It names a specific user group
It has a delivery deadline attached
It is expressed in one sentence
questions.explanation: If no test can be designed for it, the finished system cannot be evaluated against it — which is the practical purpose of SMART.

questions.stem: A project delivers on time and on budget but the problem it was built to solve persists. The correct assessment is:
options: The project failed on the criterion that matters most — the measurable outcome in the problem definition
The project succeeded, since its constraints were met
The problem definition should be revised retrospectively
The evaluation criteria were too demanding
questions.explanation: Time and budget are constraints, not objectives. Meeting them while missing the objective is a well-documented pattern.

questions.stem: The best way to keep a client genuinely involved is to:
options: Send weekly written status reports
Increase the frequency of meetings
Provide access to the code repository
Create structured opportunities — reviews and demonstrations — where feedback is given and visibly acted on
questions.explanation: Feedback that is collected and ignored damages engagement more than not asking — "enabling feedback" means closing the loop.

questions.stem: Which is the most appropriate response when a technical difficulty blocks progress?
options: Remove the feature and inform the client afterwards
Rewrite the component in a different language
Extend the deadline without consultation
Search for solutions, consult peers, and consider outsourcing the specific problem — recording the decision and its reasoning
questions.explanation: These are the named strategies for responding to development difficulties, and the record is assessable evidence of managed development.

questions.stem: Quality criteria should be defined:
options: Early, so that continual checking against them is possible throughout development
After the first working version is available for assessment
At the testing stage, when they can be measured
By the client alone, without developer input
questions.explanation: Criteria written after the fact tend to describe what was built rather than what was needed.

questions.stem: A team demonstrates a working increment each fortnight and adjusts the backlog from feedback. This is:
options: An iterative, Agile-style approach
Waterfall with staged reviews
Prototyping followed by a single release
Phased implementation
questions.explanation: (D) is a conversion method, not a development approach — the two families of term are routinely confused.

questions.stem: Which is the clearest example of preventive rather than corrective maintenance?
options: Fixing a calculation that produced the wrong total
Adjusting the system for a new operating system release
Adding a report requested by the client
Updating a library before a known vulnerability is exploited
questions.explanation: (A) is corrective, (C) perfective and (B) adaptive — all four categories appear as options.

questions.stem: The strongest concluding judgement in an evaluation of a developed solution:
options: "The solution works and the client is happy."
"The project was completed successfully within the available time."

"Against the criteria set in the problem definition, the solution is effective — handling time fell from 6 minutes to 48 seconds and double-bookings to zero — though offline capability was descoped and mobile task completion sits at 82% against a 90% target, so a responsive layout revision is recommended before the next intake."
"The solution uses appropriate technologies throughout."
questions.explanation: Criteria, measured evidence on both sides, a named limitation, and a specific recommendation tied to a decision point.

questions.stem: A project manager reduces the estimate for a task because the client will not accept the original figure. The consequence is:
options: The estimate no longer reflects reality, so the plan silently guarantees a later overrun
The schedule becomes more efficient
The critical path shortens legitimately
The contingency budget increases
questions.explanation: Negotiating the number rather than the scope moves the problem to a point where it costs more to resolve.

questions.stem: Which is the best reason to involve end-users in design rather than only the client?
options: End-users are more available for meetings
It shortens the requirements phase
End-users approve the budget
The client's understanding of daily workflow is often incomplete, and users reveal needs the specification would miss
questions.explanation: It is the practical defence against building something that verifies perfectly and validates poorly.

questions.stem: A Gantt chart shows two tasks running in parallel that in fact depend on each other. The consequence is:
options: The plan understates the project duration and the critical path is wrong
The chart becomes visually cluttered
The tasks cannot be assigned to owners
The milestones cannot be marked
questions.explanation: Missing dependencies produce a schedule that is optimistic by construction — one of the most common planning errors.

questions.stem: Which best describes the relationship between risk management and the choice of conversion method?
options: They are independent decisions
The assessed consequence of failure drives the choice — high consequence pushes toward parallel or phased
Conversion method is determined solely by budget
Risk management applies only after go-live
questions.explanation: Making that link explicit in an answer is what converts a description of four methods into a justification.

questions.stem: A team documents requirements but not the assumptions behind them. The risk is:
options: The document becomes too long
The client cannot sign off
An assumption that later proves false invalidates requirements without anyone recognising why
Testing cannot be planned
questions.explanation: Assumptions are requirements' hidden dependencies — recording them makes their failure detectable.

questions.stem: Which is the strongest argument for a data dictionary in a student project?
options: It demonstrates effort to the assessor
It is required before coding can begin
It replaces the need for an ERD
It documents each field's meaning, type, format and validation rule for anyone maintaining the system later
questions.explanation: It is technical documentation aimed at the maintainer — who, in a real project, is rarely the original author.

questions.stem: A team uses version control but commits only once a week with the message "updates". The value lost is:
options: The ability to work in parallel
Backup of the codebase
The ability to branch
Granular history, meaningful rollback points and a readable record of what changed and why
questions.explanation: Version control's benefit is proportional to the discipline applied — the tool alone provides little.

questions.stem: Which is the best example of a performance requirement?
options: "Users can cancel a booking up to 24 hours in advance"
"The system stores customer contact details"
"The booking confirmation appears within 2 seconds under 300 concurrent users"
"Administrators can export a monthly report"
questions.explanation: The others describe what the system must do — functional requirements. Performance describes how well.

questions.stem: A project's scope statement lists only inclusions. The most likely consequence is:
options: The project cannot be scheduled
Testing cannot be planned
The budget cannot be estimated
Disputes later about whether an unlisted item was implied
questions.explanation: Explicit exclusions are what make the boundary enforceable when expectations diverge.

questions.stem: Which best explains why testing should be planned from the start rather than added at the end?
options: Test design exposes ambiguity in the requirements while it is still cheap to resolve
It shortens the total project duration
It reduces the number of tests needed
It allows testing to be outsourced
questions.explanation: Writing a test forces the question "how would we know?" — which frequently reveals that the requirement cannot answer it.

questions.stem: A prototype is built, tested, and then thrown away before the real build begins. This is:
options: Evolutionary prototyping
Phased implementation
Throwaway prototyping
Incremental development
questions.explanation: Its cost is the discarded effort; its benefit is that the production system is architected properly rather than grown from a proof of concept.

questions.stem: The most useful measure of whether a change-control process is working is:
options: The number of change requests rejected
The number of changes requested per week
The speed with which changes are implemented
Whether every accepted change has a documented time and cost impact and an approval
questions.explanation: Change is legitimate; unpriced, unapproved change is what damages projects.

questions.stem: A team's velocity drops sharply after three sprints. The most useful first response is:
options: Increase the sprint length
Reduce the definition of done
Add developers to the team
Use the retrospective to identify the cause — blockers, technical debt, scope inflation or estimation drift
questions.explanation: The retrospective exists precisely for this; (C) frequently slows a team further in the short term and (B) hides the problem.

questions.stem: Which best distinguishes a milestone from a task on a Gantt chart?
options: A milestone has a duration; a task does not
A milestone marks a point in time with zero duration, usually a decision or approval
A milestone is always on the critical path
A milestone cannot have dependencies
questions.explanation: Milestones are drawn as diamonds and typically mark sign-offs, go/no-go points and releases.

questions.stem: An evaluation finds the system met every functional requirement but usage is 20% of forecast. The most useful next step is:
options: Conclude the project succeeded on its stated criteria
Investigate why — training, workflow fit, discoverability or trust — since adoption determines realised benefit
Revise the forecast retrospectively
Add more features
questions.explanation: Functional completeness without adoption produces no outcome, which is why usage belongs in the criteria set.

questions.stem: In a class diagram, the three compartments of a class rectangle are:
options: Inputs, processes, outputs
Entity, relationship, cardinality
Public, private, protected
Name, attributes, methods
questions.explanation: (B) belongs to an ERD and (A) to a system model — using the wrong notation for the wrong diagram is a common and avoidable loss.

questions.stem: The clearest sign that a project's requirements were poorly defined is:
options: The project used an Agile approach
The project used prototyping
Repeated rework caused by discovering, late, what the system was actually meant to do
The client attended every review
questions.explanation: Rework traceable to changing understanding — rather than to changing circumstances — points back to the defining stage.

questions.stem: Which statement about float is correct?
options: Tasks on the critical path have zero float by definition
Every task has float
Float can be transferred between tasks
Float increases as the project progresses
questions.explanation: That is what makes them critical — any delay propagates directly to the project end date.

questions.stem: A team implements programmed data backup within the solution. This most directly supports:
options: Usability
Accessibility conformance
Business continuity and recoverability
Performance under load
questions.explanation: It links the project work back to continuity planning — and an untested backup routine is not a backup.

questions.stem: Which is the strongest reason to present a solution to stakeholders before final sign-off?
options: It demonstrates the amount of work completed
It satisfies a documentation requirement
It surfaces disagreement and misunderstanding while change is still possible
It shortens the testing phase
questions.explanation: Presentations align stakeholders and secure decisions — their value is the disagreement they expose, not the approval they collect.

questions.stem: A student project claims "Agile was used". The strongest supporting evidence would be:
options: A statement in the report that Agile was chosen
A Gantt chart covering the whole project
Sprint records showing planned versus delivered increments, feedback received and backlog changes made as a result
A list of Agile principles
questions.explanation: Evidence of the practice, not the label. A single up-front Gantt chart covering everything (B) would tend to suggest the opposite.

questions.stem: Which is the most appropriate use of a decision tree in a project?
options: Scheduling dependent tasks
Documenting class inheritance
Showing data movement between processes
Capturing business rules and eligibility logic so the client can confirm exactly what the system will decide
questions.explanation: It makes branching logic reviewable by a non-technical stakeholder before it is implemented.

questions.stem: A system passes UAT but fails under real transaction volumes at month-end. The gap in the test plan was:
options: Boundary data
Path testing
Volume and load testing
Accessibility testing
questions.explanation: UAT confirms fitness for purpose under normal use; behaviour at peak volume is a separate, deliberately designed test.

questions.stem: Which best describes the purpose of a driver in testing?
options: It calls the module under test so it can be exercised before the surrounding system exists
It stands in for a module that has not yet been written
It generates random test data
It records test results automatically
questions.explanation: (B) describes a stub — the two are complements and are routinely swapped in answers.

questions.stem: A team writes a test case with an input but no expected result. The consequence is:
options: There is nothing to compare the actual output against, so the test can neither pass nor fail meaningfully
The test cannot be automated
The test is invalid for boundary data
The test cannot be traced to a requirement
questions.explanation: Documented expected results are what convert running the software into testing it.

questions.stem: Which is the most defensible reason to reject a client's requested feature?
options: The team finds it technically uninteresting
It conflicts with a legal or accessibility obligation, and an alternative achieving the same goal is proposed
It would extend the timeline
It was not in the original brief
questions.explanation: (C) and (D) are matters for negotiation rather than rejection — and offering an alternative is what makes the refusal constructive.

questions.stem: A project's communication plan should specify:
options: The programming languages used
The test data categories
Who is told what, through which channel, at what frequency, and who decides
The class diagram notation
questions.explanation: It prevents the two most common failures — stakeholders learning of problems too late, and decisions made without the people who must live with them.

questions.stem: An implementation plan includes training but not a support arrangement for the first fortnight. The likely consequence is:
options: The training budget will be underspent
Users encountering their first real edge cases have nowhere to turn, and workarounds become entrenched
The conversion method must change
Documentation will become outdated
questions.explanation: Habits formed in week one persist — which is why floor-walking support is disproportionately valuable.

questions.stem: Which best describes the relationship between verification and validation activities across a project?
options: Validation occurs first, then verification
They are performed by the same people at the same time
Verification runs throughout against the specification; validation confirms the specification was right
Verification applies only to code and validation only to documentation
questions.explanation: Building it right versus building the right thing — and a system can fully satisfy the first while failing the second.

questions.stem: A project's greatest source of avoidable cost is usually:
options: Software licensing
Hardware procurement
Rework caused by defects and misunderstandings discovered late
Documentation production
questions.explanation: It is the same shift-left argument that drives early testing, prototyping and stakeholder involvement.

questions.stem: Which is the best measure of whether a process diary is serving its purpose?
options: The number of entries made
Whether entries were made daily
Whether the entries record decisions, their reasoning, and what changed as a result
The total word count
questions.explanation: Frequency and length are proxies; the reasoning is what makes the record evaluable.

questions.stem: A client insists on a feature the team believes will harm usability. The best professional response is:
options: Present evidence from usability testing, propose an alternative meeting the same goal, and document the final decision
Implement it without comment, since the client decides
Refuse to implement it
Implement it but hide it in the interface
questions.explanation: Responding appropriately to stakeholders means balancing what the client wants against evidence — then recording the decision either way.

questions.stem: Which is the strongest indicator that a project's scope has crept?
options: Delivered functionality has grown without corresponding changes to time, budget or documented agreement
The client has requested changes
The Gantt chart has been revised
New risks have been identified
questions.explanation: Change is normal; unrecorded, unpriced growth is scope creep.

questions.stem: The most useful thing a team can do in the first week of a project is:
options: Begin coding the most complex module
Select the development framework
Establish the problem definition, boundaries and measurable success criteria with the client
Draft the user manual
questions.explanation: Every later decision — approach, method, tests, evaluation — depends on it, and a defect here is the most expensive kind.

questions.stem: A team schedules integration testing before all modules are complete. This is possible because of:
options: Stubs and drivers
Regression testing
Path testing
Boundary analysis
questions.explanation: Stubs stand in for what a module calls; drivers call the module — together they decouple testing from build order.

questions.stem: Which is the most accurate statement about documentation types?
options: User documentation explains how to operate the system; technical documentation explains how it works
User documentation explains internal structure; technical documentation explains operation
They are interchangeable if written well
Only technical documentation is assessable
questions.explanation: (B) is the pair inverted. Both are required, and they serve genuinely different audiences.

questions.stem: An evaluation that lists what the system does, without judgement, will typically:
options: Score well because it demonstrates knowledge
Score well provided limitations are omitted
Score well if it is comprehensive
Score in the lower bands, because "evaluate" requires criteria, evidence and a conclusion
questions.explanation: Description without judgement is the single most common way to lose marks on an extended response.

questions.stem: Which piece of evidence would best support a claim that a project was cost-effective?
options: The team worked long hours to deliver it
Actual versus budgeted cost, plus quantified benefit and a payback period including ongoing operating cost
The client thanked the team
The system uses free open-source components
questions.explanation: Cost-effectiveness is a ratio — both sides must be quantified, and the denominator must include ongoing cost.

questions.stem: The clearest sign of a mature approach to feedback is:
options: Feedback is collected at the end of the project
Feedback is recorded verbatim in the process diary
Feedback is collected from every stakeholder equally
Feedback is synthesised into a report, prioritised, acted on, and the resulting change is recorded and re-tested
questions.explanation: Collection is the easy half; the loop is closed by the change and its verification.

questions.stem: Across the whole project, the strongest evidence of professional practice is:
options: Planned versus actual tracking, version control history, documented decisions with reasoning, criteria-based evaluation and demonstrated response to feedback
A large and technically impressive codebase
Early completion ahead of schedule
Adoption of the newest available frameworks
questions.explanation: These are exactly what the outcomes ask you to apply methods to manage, document and evaluate — and they are assessable in a way a finished artefact alone is not.
